Photograph: Kostiantyn Liberov/Libkos/Getty Images Ukraine Russia strikes at heart of Ukraine’s digital economy with attacks on ISPs and datacentres As winter approaches, Kyiv fears disruption to vital networks that keep banks, payment systems and public services running Ukraine and Russia’s long-range drone war Pjotr Sauer in Kyiv Sat 26 Sep 2026 00.00 EDT Last modified on Sat 26 Sep 2026 00.02 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Russia has opened a new front in its campaign against Ukraine , hitting several datacentres and internet providers in Kyiv this week in an apparent attempt to weaken the digital backbone of the economy. About 100,000 households in Kyiv and the surrounding region suffered temporary internet outages after strikes on Wednesday and Thursday, according to Ukraine’s digital transformation ministry. On Friday, another drone strike in central Kyiv hit the offices of Datagroup, one of Ukraine’s largest telecommunications companies, killing four people. “Russia has targeted major Ukrainian datacentres, seeking to disrupt the flow of information,” Ukraine’s foreign minister, Andrii Sybiha, wrote on X. On Thursday, Polish authorities reported a Starlink satellite station in central Poland serving Ukraine had been set on fire , in what appeared to be part of a coordinated attack on Ukraine’s internet infrastructure. Local officials described it as an “act of sabotage” linked to Moscow. Russia has previously targeted Ukraine’s datacentres, but attacks on this scale are new. Russia could attack a Nato country within months, Danish intelligence says Read more Keeping the country connected has been a priority for the Ukrainian government throughout the war, with authorities looking for ways to ensure mobile and internet providers have enough backup power to keep operating during prolonged electricity outages. Ukraine’s relatively decentralised internet network also makes it harder for individual strikes to cause widespread or prolonged outages across whole cities or regions. But with winter approaching, officials and industry figures fear repeated Russian attacks could begin to disrupt the networks that keep Ukraine’s banks, payment systems and public services running. “I recommend Kyiv residents gradually prepare for winter … by getting Starlink terminals or other means of maintaining communications,” Serhii Sternenko, a popular blogger and former government adviser, wrote on X. “The goal of the Russians is not only to strike at the capital’s energy infrastructure but also to destroy all datacentres and internet operators,” Sternenko added. The attacks come amid Russia’s intensified strikes on Ukraine’s economy , with missiles and new jet-powered drones used against warehouses, petrol stations, ports and other commercial infrastructure, adding further pressure to an economy already strained by nearly five years of full-scale war. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Weekly Sign up to This is Europe The most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environment after newsletter promotion View image in fullscreen On Friday, Russia struck a warehouse used by the McDonald’s chain. Photograph: Sergiy Chalyi/Reuters Among the targets on Friday was a warehouse used by the McDonald’s fast food restaurant chain outside Kyiv. Heavy industry has also been hit hard, with Russian strikes disrupting industrial facilities and steel production. This month, Ukraine failed to produce a single tonne of steel for the first time in a century, according to a senior industry official. Ukraine is struggling to counter a growing wave of new high-speed Russian jet-powered drones, including the Geran-5, while also running critically low on Patriot missiles needed to defend against Russian ballistic and cruise missile attacks. Speaking to reporters on Friday, the Ukrainian president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, said Donald Trump had approved granting Ukraine licences to produce Patriot air defence missiles, potentially giving Kyiv a path to manufacture the crucial systems domestically, though experts say it could take years to establish production. Trump has previously flip-flopped over whether to allow Ukraine to produce Patriots, with the US also facing pressure on its own stocks because of the war in the Middle East. Trump announced unilaterally on social media on Sunday evening that "both parties" had agreed to an "energy ceasefire" which was "effective immediately." There was no immediate ​confirmation ⁠from Moscow and Zelenskyy told the news site Axios within minutes of Trump's claim that the ceasefire was "news for me." Ukrainian energy facility attacked On Monday morning, Zelenskyy told the annual Warsaw Security Forum that there had been "Russian ​violations of the energy ​ceasefire announced President Trump" overnight, while the mayor of the northeastern city of Kharkiv reporting at least 12 injuries in attacks on energy facilities. "It was clear that [Russian President Vladimir] Putin does not read Truth Social," Zelenskyy said, referring to Trump's social media platform. "If Russia wants us to stop our long-range strikes against its oil refineries and oil exports, then it must stop its strikes against our energy system and critical infrastructure and stop killing our people," he said via video link, adding that he learned about the apparent ceasefire through the media. "This ceasefire, it can work, and it can ​become ⁠a major step toward ending the war if ⁠the ​Americans truly step in now and make sure Russians respect it," he said. "We are waiting for the ​of the conditions between the Americans and Russians, and we are waiting to ​see one specific step the Americans are ready to take. "If Russia does not agree to an energy ceasefire, we will respond." EU: No sign of Russia sticking to ceasefire The European Union 's foreign affairs chief Kaja Kallas said on Monday at a meeting of EU foreign ministers in Luxembourg that the bloc would "welcome the energy ceasefire if it holds" but added: "We haven't yet seen that Russia will also stick to it." French President Emmanuel Macron also insisted that a "real ceasefire" be "respected by both sides" but said: "I ​have ⁠not noted, over the last 48 ⁠hours, ​any energy ceasefire coming from the Russian side." The Russian government said on Monday that President Putin would only consider a ceasefire for a single day in the event that Ukraine intended to hold a presidential election. The Kremlin earlier rejected ​a 60-day election ceasefire idea proposed by ⁠President ​Zelenskyy. "I do not think he deserves a respite," said Russian Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov.
